vignette:
At thirty-five, he speaks softly and precisely, with the careful attention to detail that fits his work as a UX designer. He is a married South Eastern Asian man who spends his days thinking about flow, friction, and what makes people feel safe enough to move through a system. When he talks about the year he became seriously ill, it is striking how quickly that sense of safety disappeared from his own life.

Before the illness, he describes himself as busy, dependable, and “always in planning mode.” He works long hours, sketches interface ideas on scraps of paper, and jokes with his wife that he can redesign anything except their overflowing kitchen drawer. He is healthy by his own account, the kind of person who ignores minor symptoms and assumes his body will cooperate. That changes after what begins as fatigue, fever, and abdominal pain. At first he tries to work through it from home, laptop open beside him on the couch, telling his team he just needs a day or two. But within days, his condition worsens rapidly. He remembers the bright hospital lights, the cold rush of being wheeled through hallways, and the look on his wife’s face when staff start moving faster and talking in clipped, serious tones. He understands enough to know that something is badly wrong. He says the fear begins not with pain, but with the moment he realizes he may actually die.

During the hospitalization, time becomes fragmented. He remembers alarms, masks, needles, forms he cannot concentrate on, and the helplessness of needing other people for everything. He remembers trying to read staff members’ faces for clues, searching for reassurance and finding only practiced neutrality. At night he lies awake listening to machines and the footsteps in the corridor, convinced that each new sound means another emergency. He starts imagining his wife going home alone, having to explain to family what happened. He thinks about unfinished work files, passwords no one else knows, small domestic things that suddenly feel unbearable because they suggest he might not return to them. Even after the worst of the medical crisis passes, his body feels unfamiliar and untrustworthy. He says that while everyone around him seems relieved he survived, he does not feel relief so much as shock.

When he comes home, his family expects recovery to mean gratitude and rest. Instead, he becomes watchful and easily startled. He wakes suddenly in the dark, heart racing, sure for a few seconds that he is back in the hospital bed and something has gone wrong. The sound of his phone vibrating on the nightstand jolts him. Monitoring devices in medical dramas on television make his chest tighten. He avoids follow-up portals and delays opening lab results because seeing medical language on a screen makes him nauseous. His wife notices that he keeps asking if she thinks he looks pale, if his breathing seems normal, if she hears anything unusual in his voice. He checks his pulse often, sometimes counting it through entire meetings while trying to look engaged on camera.

Returning to work is harder than he expects. Before the illness, he enjoys solving design problems and advocating for users. Now he finds himself preoccupied by worst-case scenarios. If a colleague says, “Can you hop on a quick call?” he feels a surge of dread, as if bad news is coming. He loses time staring at health articles instead of wireframes. In design reviews, when discussions become fast or overlapping, his mind goes blank and he struggles to follow. He has always been known for calm presentation, but now his hands sweat when he shares his screen. He becomes unusually rigid about contingency planning, wanting every feature to have fail-safes, backup paths, explicit warnings. He recognizes that some of this comes from his job, but even he can tell it has intensified beyond usefulness. He is no longer just designing for ease; he is trying to eliminate catastrophe.

At home, his world grows smaller. He avoids hospitals altogether except when absolutely necessary. Routes that pass the emergency department make him tense and silent. He stops exercising because any increase in heart rate feels dangerous. When his wife gets a cold, he becomes irritable and overprotective, wiping surfaces repeatedly and sleeping lightly so he can listen for changes in her breathing. He feels ashamed of how much reassurance he needs and embarrassed by how angry he becomes when people tell him he is “lucky” or suggest he should be over it because the illness is finished. To him, it is not finished. It lives in his body as a constant expectation of collapse.

He still goes to work, still makes dinner with his wife some evenings, still answers messages from friends with polite delay. On the surface, his life has resumed. But he moves through it as if danger is layered just beneath ordinary things. A headache is not a headache; it is a warning. A routine checkup is not routine; it is a doorway back into terror. He says he misses the version of himself who could make plans without first imagining how everything might unravel. What stays with him most is not only that he nearly died, but that he learned, in a way he cannot unlearn, how quickly life can turn unfamiliar and how little control he really has.
